Roughly two months ago I met two people who have had an immeasurable impact on my work in the last two months. 

First off, Anna Ursin. Anna kindly spent an hour with Pinja Dodik and I in late March, sharing a no-holds-barred, whistlestop tour of how she uses Claude Code to 10x her go-to-market efforts (think: less AI slop, more AI system). 

Since that conversation, or rather, since the Easter weekend after where I *finally* found a couple of days to build out my Claude Code "OS", I have spent probably 80% of my working time tinkering, wibbling, and booping in VS Code (is this Claudative determinism?) 

As someone who thrives on context, subtext and synthesis (lit grad here, soz), I thought AI was coming for my favourite things. But switching to this more systemic approach has helped me apply those favourite things to my set-up. 

I still have *so much* to learn, but compared to 60 days ago, I'm flying. Anna's generosity has inspired me to keep learning, and to pay it forward by hosting my own Claude sharing session in Valencia tomorrow. 

Thanks so much Anna, and if you're a SaaS company with 1-5M ARR looking for GTM consultant: you know where to go. 

Second off, Peter Townsend joined the marketing team in late March and has hit the ground running when it comes to taking all our events and campaigns off my hands. He's already smashed the targets for our OSS AI Studio webinar, and is looking on track to do the same for our latest MCP Gateway webinar on 21 May (links in comments). 

And by doing such a sterling job, he's freed me up to spend more time building out new solutions to support the team. Great to have you on board, Peter! 

A final special shout out to Pinja Dodik at Swarmia for being the marketer I learn most from - and who intro'd me to Anna (case in point!) So glad we connected many LinkedIn years ago 🤗

Being invited onto Claudia Noriega-Bernstein's podcast, Don't Shrink to Fit™, was one of those conversations I knew would matter the moment it began.

Claudia opened with a story that stopped me. A news report from Las Vegas, two 15-year-olds facing charges for deeply disturbing behaviour. But rather than reacting with shock, she asked a far harder question: what were the signs we missed long before that day?

Behaviour is rarely the root. It is almost always the last thing we see after a child's nervous system has been quietly asking for help for a very long time.

This is precisely why I built HushAway®.

So much of what gets labelled as "difficult" in children, particularly neurodivergent children, is a nervous system trying to find safety in a world that feels too fast, too loud, and too unpredictable. Regulation is not woo-woo, and it is not optional. It is the foundation that learning, sleep, confidence and connection are built upon.

In this episode, Claudia and I explored:

- Why behaviour is the last expression, not the root problem
- Why co-regulation (how WE show up) teaches a child's nervous system more than any instruction ever could
- How sound, storytelling and predictability help children feel safe enough to settle
- Why awareness, presence and curiosity matter far more than perfection

Claudia is a rare kind of host. She holds the hardest truths with real warmth, and this was one of the most grounded, honest interviews I've had about what our children genuinely need from us right now.

If you are a parent, an educator, or anyone who loves a child who feels things deeply, I think you will find something in this conversation worth holding onto.

🎧 Watch the full episode on Spotify - link in the comments.

With huge thanks to Claudia for the invitation, and for the space she creates for conversations like this.

So something I've been thinking about a lot lately.
Most employee wellness programmes in the GCC are imported. Designed in the West, translated with a few arabic words, then delivered here. And I think that's why most people here are living like permanently exhausted pigeons.

A lot of wellness culture is obsessed with outcomes. Track your calories Hit your macros. Measure your sleep score. Optimize your work by walking as you work. Count your steps. Everything is a metric. Everything is a result. 
But...I believe that's not how this region thinks or works. It's just not how this culture is wired.

We come from a tradition that was built on balance long before wellness became an industry. You plant the seed, set the right environment for it to grow and then ideally the fruits just come...and sometimes they don't... You show up to work with full sincerity and give it your best; the rizq is written anyway. You tie the camel and then leave it to Allah. 

That's actually what prevents burnout and restlessness, no? The simple understanding that what was meant for you will reach you as long as you put the effort and also that sometimes you could do all the right things but the result was not the fruit itself but who you transformed into as you did all those right things. 

And this burnout extends to families too. As a counsellor and coach, I see it way too often that teens these days are lonely and withdrawn..disinterested in life...mostly because parents [aka the employees+employers] are working around the clock or outsourcing care. 

Yes....There are multiple dimensions to this...but if there is one place to start, it is the individual..the internal clock...one's own rhythm. And when multiple individuals come together, it's bound to bring larger change.

There is now a profession on LinkedIn called VibeCode Cleaner. 

That tells you everything you need to know about where we are. 

These are people who get hired to fix projects after vibe coders are done with them. Usually the projects where API keys got exposed, systems got breached, and someone already real money or wants to avoid that. 

Yes, if you're lucky, with vibe coding you can do something in 20 minutes that would have taken days otherwise. 

But what if you're not lucky... 
(And the odds are not in your favor.)

I see again and again that people treat this as a speed decision. Move fast, skip the review, deal with problems later. But then your database is half-gone or your infrastructure is compromised, and just a mess you don't fully understand. 

Vibe coding has a legitimate use case: prototypes, proof of concepts. 

But production code is not a vibe. If the code is supposed to run in production, be maintained, and scale – a specific person has to own it.

The paradox: the fastest way to go fast is to go slightly slower: review every line, validate every step, and never generate more than you can check. 

Otherwise you're not moving fast. (But the cleaner with a new job thanks you, though.)

日本の「反戦姿勢」の転換と、米中対立の裏側に潜む日本の外交危機

先日、BBCが「日本の反戦姿勢の見直し」について報じました。
高市政権下で憲法改正の動きが加速し、国内では抗議行動も拡大しています。
しかし、この議論の表面だけを見ていては、
日本が直面している真の危機を見誤ることに
なります。
今、私たちが直面しているのは、単なる「改憲か護憲か」という国内問題ではなく、世界の外交戦略のリアリズムに対する「日本の読み違い」という深刻な課題です。
1. 米中が見せる「正面衝突を避ける」リアリズム
現在の米中関係を「単純な対立」と捉えるのは早計です。外交戦略の観点から見れば、両国は互いに激しい言葉で非難し合いながらも、経済や安全保障の致命的なラインにおいては、決して相手を正面から決定的に破綻させるような批判は行いません。
彼らは「対立」さえも自国の利益を最大化するための外交カードとして使い分けています。互いの腹の内を探り合い、実利を確保するためには裏で握り合う。これが現代のグローバル外交の冷徹なスタンダードです。
2. 日本に欠如している「主権者意識」という
根源的課題
こうした米中の高度な駆け引きに対し、日本はどうでしょうか。
私が最も危惧しているのは、日本人の「主権者意識」の希薄さです。その象徴が「日米地位協定」の改定議論が遅々として進まない現状にあります。
戦後80年近くが経過してもなお、不平等な協定が放置されている。その背景には、政府による「日米同盟こそが唯一の正解である」という巧妙な宣伝活動（プロパガンダ）の影響が否定できません。国民が「主権者」として自国の不条理を是正しようとする意識を、安全保障という美名の下で事実上抑制されてきたのではないか、という視点が必要です。
3. 外交戦略の「読み間違い」が招く最悪のシナリオ
もし日本が、米中の表面的な対立構造だけを

国際社会での日本の立ち位置は相対的に低下し、気がついた時には他国の戦略的利益の「調整弁」として使われかねません。
4. 今、私たちに求められるもの
今こそ、私たちは「宣伝」の裏側を見抜く力を持たなければなりません。

• 多角的な外交インテリジェンス: 報道の表面をなぞるのではなく、米中の実利に基づいた動きを冷徹に分析すること。
日本が国際社会で真の自立を果たし、強靭な国益を確保するためには、感情的な議論を排し、この冷徹な外交リアリズムに立ち返ることが不可欠です。

Just a thought that’s been sitting in my mind lately... and honestly, it feels worth discussing openly.

The internet quietly changed the psychology of growth!

Most businesses haven’t fully realized it yet.

There was a time when scaling revenue felt mechanical:

- Build lists.
- Hire BDRs.
- Increase outbound volume.
- Optimize scripts.
- Book meetings.

And for years, that system worked brilliantly.

Because attention was still scarce.

An email felt personal.
A LinkedIn message felt intentional.
Outreach still carried signal.

But then the market evolved.

Every company gained access to automation.
Then personalization at scale.
Then AI-generated messaging.

Now everyone can reach everyone.

Which created an unexpected consequence:

Attention lost value!

The more businesses tried to manufacture relevance…
the more audiences learned to emotionally filter everything out.

Especially high-value clients.

That’s why many traditional growth systems feel weaker today, even when the tools are technically “better.”

The issue isn’t sales.
It isn’t outbound.
And it definitely isn’t talent.

The issue is that modern buyers no longer respond primarily to pursuit.

They respond to perception.

The companies winning today often create trust before the first conversation ever happens.

Their positioning travels ahead of them.
Their reputation pre-sells them.
Their authority reduces friction before outreach even begins.

In other words:

Growth is no longer just a distribution problem.

It’s becoming a credibility architecture problem.

And that changes everything.

Because when markets become saturated with noise, the advantage no longer belongs to whoever speaks the loudest…

It belongs to whoever feels impossible to ignore.

Maybe that’s the real shift happening right now.

We’re moving from the era of aggressive acquisition…

into the era of perceived inevitability.

The companies that thrive next won’t just generate leads.

They’ll shape perception so effectively that trust already exists before the first touchpoint even happens.

That’s a very different game.

Je n’ai pas l’habitude de prendre la parole sur ce type de sujet ici sur LinkedIn. Pourtant, je suis convaincu qu’il est essentiel de s’exprimer sur cette question aujourd’hui.

Le Conseil d’État examine actuellement un projet de loi visant à revoir l’organisation des antennes locales de l'ADEME, en les rattachant aux DREAL (Directions régionales de l’environnement, de l’aménagement et du logement) et, de fait, en les plaçant sous l’autorité des préfets.

Cette réforme entraînerait un affaiblissement majeur de l’agence, notamment parce que :
1.  Le réseau régional sur lequel l’ADEME s’appuie pour faire avancer des milliers de projets locaux en faveur de l’écologie se retrouverait soumis au pouvoir hiérarchique des préfets. Les priorités ne seraient alors plus guidées par l’urgence écologique, mais davantage par celles du ministère de l’Intérieur.
2.  La suppression des agences territoriales provoquerait une dilution des compétences, de l’expertise et de l’efficacité des équipes, au sein de structures ne disposant ni du savoir-faire technique et scientifique nécessaire, ni de l’ancrage local auprès des élus et porteurs de projets.

Même si ces deux points peuvent paraître abstraits pour beaucoup, cette proposition est surtout le signe visible d’une intention plus large : affaiblir le rôle de l’ADEME, dénigrer son activité et minimiser sa contribution à l’avancement de la transition écologique.
L’ADEME, ce n’est pas seulement une institution. C’est un soutien concret à travers des financements pour des projets locaux, des ressources digitales, des études, des guides, des formations et des données accessibles librement.
Il est donc important que chacun — et encore plus les personnes dont le métier consiste à contribuer à la transition écologique — soit informé de ce qu’il se passe et prenne position.

Je fais donc appel à mon réseau, même modeste, pour mobiliser un maximum de personnes et alerter sur ce sujet.

Voici quelques actions concrètes possibles :
1. Écrire à vos sénateurs et députés locaux.
2. Relayer le sujet sur les réseaux sociaux et soutenir les publications existantes.
3. Diffuser l’appel à témoignages : https://lnkd.in/dgU5FCJf
4. Partager la tribune sur le sujet, déjà soutenue par plus de 400 signataires : https://lnkd.in/dQnB7-yc 
5. Utiliser le kit de mobilisation conçu par Gabrielle Piot pour faciliter le passage à l’action.


PS : Merci à toi Gabrielle d'avoir lancé cette mobilisation !!

若くから活躍でき、年収が高い会社というイメージのサイバーエージェント。 2025年最新の情報をもとに、同社の平均年収や年齢・職種・役職別の年収目安、評価制度、福利厚生などについて解説します。 元社員への取材をもとに、リアルな年収事情をお伝えします。尚、記事中の情報は記事作成当時のものです。ご了承ください。 ■サイバーエージェントの平均年収は913万円 2025年9月の有価証券報告書によると、従業員数約2,588名、平均年齢33.8歳、平均勤続年数6.5年、平均年間給与は913.8万円です。年収はここ数年右肩上がりでアップしています。 ■【属性別】サイバーエージェントの年収目安 サイバーエージェントは新卒の初任給も業界トップクラスです。年齢にかかわらず成果を出せば昇給できる実力主義の風土があり、20代で400万～980万円、30代で700万～1,000万円以上、40代で770万～1,000万円以上が目安です。 サイバーエージェントでは職種によって年収レンジが異なり、マーケティング職が平均年収721万円、エンジニア職・SE職が670万円、営業職が661万円となっています。クリエイター職はスキル次第で、デザイナー職の平均年収は552万円です。 一般社員からチーフ、マネージャー、部長、局長と昇進するにつれて年収も大きく上昇します。マネージャーに昇格すると800万～1,000万円、部長や局長クラスでは1,500万円以上、さらにエグゼクティブや役員、取締役になると報酬は数千万円規模になります。 ■サイバーエージェントで年収1000万円は可能？実現のキャリアパス 多くの社員が30代で年収1,000万円の水準に到達し、時には若くして子会社の社長や役員に抜擢されることもあります。専門職として高い技術力を評価される、マネージャーとして成果を出す、営業力で実績を上げてインセンティブを得るなど、高年収を目指すことは可能です。 ■サイバーエージェントと競合の年収比較 サイバーエージェント（913万円 平均年齢33.8歳）は電通（1507.5万円 44.9歳）、博報堂（1091.5万円 41.4歳）に次ぐ高い平均年収です。平均年齢が非常に若く、若くして高年収が期待できる環境です。 ■サイバーエージェント中途入社者の年収実績 サイバーエージェントに転職することで、年収が高い大手からの転職は年収維持、専門性はあるが年収が低めな専業代理店からの転職は年収アップ、大手企業でリーダー層を経験し、年収800万円程度に達している人材は1,000万円を突破できる可能性が高いです。事業開発などの重要ポストでは高額な報酬を用意して経験者を採用しています ■サイバーエージェントの給与はどのように決まる？評価制度を解説 サイバーエージェントの給与形態は年俸制です。年に一度提示される年俸額を12分割し、月々の基本給として支給され、一般的な企業のような夏と冬の定期ボーナスはありません。 昇給は年に2回、半期ごとに行われる評価査定の結果に基づいて決定されます。業績が好調な年度には、社員に利益を還元する目的で決算賞与が支給されることがあります。 年収には一定時間分のみなし残業代が含まれ、既定の時間を超えて残業した場合はその超過分の残業代が別途支給されます。みなし残業代は職種や等級によって異なるため、内定時に労働条件通知書で詳細を確認することが重要です。 サイバーエージェントの評価は目標管理制度（MBO）に基づいて行われ、期初に設定した目標の達成度や業務への貢献度を自己評価と上長評価によって決定されます。営業職の場合、成績が良い人はインセンティブも付与されて年収がどんどん上がっていきます。また、会社が力を入れている事業に携わっている人が良い評価を受けやすい傾向にあるようです。 逆に、半期ごとの評価で期待される成果を出せなかった場合、昇給が見送られ年収が上がらないことがあります。 ■サイバーエージェント営業職のリアルな年収と査定 取材した元社員の入社1年目に408万円でスタートした年収は、2年目に446万円にアップしました。その内訳は、半期の査定でA評価（＋3万円）、B評価（＋1万円）、月ごとの目標達成6回（＋4万円ｘ6か月分）、目標達成率社内1位が1回（＋10万円）です。 現在の新卒スタート年収は504万円と大幅にアップしている上、インセンティブの額も現在とは異なりますが、査定によって順調に年収がアップするシステムです。 ■家賃補助など年収以外の魅力も！サイバーエージェント独自の福利厚生 勤務地の最寄り駅から2駅以内に住むと月3万円の家賃補助が受けられる「2駅ルール」、勤続年数5年を超えた正社員はどこに住んでも5万円が補助される「どこでもルール」が有名です。 女性社員の活躍を支援する制度「macalon」の他、有給取得のしやすさや勤続年数に応じたリフレッシュ休暇など、長期的に働きやすい環境が整っており、離職率の低下につながっています。 ■中途採用で入社した場合、初年度の年収の決まり方 前職での給与や、これまでの経験・スキルをもとに個別の交渉を通じて年収が決定されます。中途採用では即戦力が求められるため、高い専門性を持つ経験者ほど好待遇が期待できます。求人の採用難易度によっても提示額は変動し、未経験からの転職では前職より年収が下がるケースがあります。 サイバーエージェントの年収 や評価制度などについて詳報しております。記事全文をぜひご覧ください。 Being invited onto Claudia Noriega-Bernstein's podcast, Don't Shrink to Fit™, was one of those conversations I knew would matter the moment it began.

Claudia opened with a story that stopped me. A news report from Las Vegas, two 15-year-olds facing charges for deeply disturbing behaviour. But rather than reacting with shock, she asked a far harder question: what were the signs we missed long before that day?

Behaviour is rarely the root. It is almost always the last thing we see after a child's nervous system has been quietly asking for help for a very long time.

This is precisely why I built HushAway®.

So much of what gets labelled as "difficult" in children, particularly neurodivergent children, is a nervous system trying to find safety in a world that feels too fast, too loud, and too unpredictable. Regulation is not woo-woo, and it is not optional. It is the foundation that learning, sleep, confidence and connection are built upon.

In this episode, Claudia and I explored:

- Why behaviour is the last expression, not the root problem
- Why co-regulation (how WE show up) teaches a child's nervous system more than any instruction ever could
- How sound, storytelling and predictability help children feel safe enough to settle
- Why awareness, presence and curiosity matter far more than perfection

Claudia is a rare kind of host. She holds the hardest truths with real warmth, and this was one of the most grounded, honest interviews I've had about what our children genuinely need from us right now.

If you are a parent, an educator, or anyone who loves a child who feels things deeply, I think you will find something in this conversation worth holding onto.

With huge thanks to Claudia for the invitation, and for the space she creates for conversations like this.

So something I've been thinking about a lot lately.
 Why are most people here living like permanently exhausted pigeons?

A lot of wellness culture is obsessed with outcomes. Track your calories Hit your macros. Measure your sleep score. Optimize your work by walking as you work. Count your steps. Everything is a metric. Everything is a result. 
But...I believe that's not how this region thinks or works. It's just not how this culture is wired.
Most employee wellness programmes in the GCC are imported. Designed in the West, translated with a few arabic words, then delivered here. And I think
We come from a tradition that was built on balance long before wellness became an industry. 

You plant the seed, set the right environment for it to grow and then ideally the fruits just come...and sometimes they don't... You show up to work with full sincerity and give it your best; the rizq is written anyway. You tie the camel and then leave it to Allah. 

That's actually what prevents burnout and restlessness, no? The simple understanding that what was meant for you will reach you as long as you put the effort and also that sometimes you could do all the right things but the result was not the fruit itself but who you transformed into as you did all those right things. 

And this burnout extends to families too. As a counsellor and coach, I see it way too often that teens these days are lonely and withdrawn..disinterested in life...mostly because parents [aka the employees+employers] are working around the clock or outsourcing care.

There is now a profession on LinkedIn called VibeCode Cleaner. 

That tells you everything you need to know about where we are. 

These are people who get hired to fix projects after vibe coders are done with them. Usually the projects where API keys got exposed, systems got breached, and someone already real money or wants to avoid that. 

Yes, if you're lucky, with vibe coding you can do something in 20 minutes that would have taken days otherwise. 

But what if you're not lucky... 
(And the odds are not in your favor.)

I see again and again that people treat this as a speed decision. Move fast, skip the review, deal with problems later. But then your database is half-gone or your infrastructure is compromised, and just a mess you don't fully understand. 

Vibe coding has a legitimate use case: prototypes, proof of concepts. 

But production code is not a vibe. If the code is supposed to run in production, be maintained, and scale – a specific person has to own it.

The paradox: the fastest way to go fast is to go slightly slower: review every line, validate every step, and never generate more than you can check. 

Otherwise you're not moving fast. (But the cleaner with a new job thanks you, though.)

Today I had the privilege of presenting our work on electrohydrodynamic (EHD) propulsion systems at JAIN (Deemed-to-be University), Department of Aerospace Engineering.

What is Ionic Propulsion? Imagine aircraft that fly without engines, propellers, or any moving parts. 日本の「反戦姿勢」の転換と、米中対立の裏側に潜む日本の外交危機

先日、BBCが「日本の反戦姿勢の見直し」について報じました。
高市政権下で憲法改正の動きが加速し、国内では抗議行動も拡大しています。
しかし、この議論の表面だけを見ていては、
日本が直面している真の危機を見誤ることに
なります。
今、私たちが直面しているのは、単なる「改憲か護憲か」という国内問題ではなく、世界の外交戦略のリアリズムに対する「日本の読み違い」という深刻な課題です。
1. 米中が見せる「正面衝突を避ける」リアリズム
現在の米中関係を「単純な対立」と捉えるのは早計です。外交戦略の観点から見れば、両国は互いに激しい言葉で非難し合いながらも、経済や安全保障の致命的なラインにおいては、決して相手を正面から決定的に破綻させるような批判は行いません。
彼らは「対立」さえも自国の利益を最大化するための外交カードとして使い分けています。互いの腹の内を探り合い、実利を確保するためには裏で握り合う。これが現代のグローバル外交の冷徹なスタンダードです。
2. 日本に欠如している「主権者意識」という
根源的課題
こうした米中の高度な駆け引きに対し、日本はどうでしょうか。
私が最も危惧しているのは、日本人の「主権者意識」の希薄さです。その象徴が「日米地位協定」の改定議論が遅々として進まない現状にあります。
戦後80年近くが経過してもなお、不平等な協定が放置されている。その背景には、政府による「日米同盟こそが唯一の正解である」という巧妙な宣伝活動（プロパガンダ）の影響が否定できません。国民が「主権者」として自国の不条理を是正しようとする意識を、安全保障という美名の下で事実上抑制されてきたのではないか、という視点が必要です。
3. 外交戦略の「読み間違い」が招く最悪のシナリオ
もし日本が、米中の表面的な対立構造だけを
真に受け、彼らの「裏の握り」や「戦略的抑制」を読み違えれば、日本は大変な状況に追い込まれる可能性があります。
「反戦」や「改憲」という感情的な議論に終始し、政府の宣伝に踊らされている間に、

Just a thought that’s been sitting in my mind lately... and honestly, it feels worth discussing openly.

The internet quietly changed the psychology of growth!

Most businesses haven’t fully realized it yet.

There was a time when scaling revenue felt mechanical:

- Build lists.
- Hire BDRs.
- Increase outbound volume.
- Optimize scripts.
- Book meetings.

And for years, that system worked brilliantly.

Because attention was still scarce.

An email felt personal.
A LinkedIn message felt intentional.
Outreach still carried signal.

But then the market evolved.

Every company gained access to automation.
Then personalization at scale.
Then AI-generated messaging.

Now everyone can reach everyone.

Which created an unexpected consequence:

Attention lost value!

The more businesses tried to manufacture relevance…
the more audiences learned to emotionally filter everything out.

Especially high-value clients.

That’s why many traditional growth systems feel weaker today, even when the tools are technically “better.”

The issue isn’t sales.
It isn’t outbound.
And it definitely isn’t talent.

The issue is that modern buyers no longer respond primarily to pursuit.

They respond to perception.

The companies winning today often create trust before the first conversation ever happens.

Their positioning travels ahead of them.
Their reputation pre-sells them.
Their authority reduces friction before outreach even begins.

In other words:

Growth is no longer just a distribution problem.

It’s becoming a credibility architecture problem.

And that changes everything.

Because when markets become saturated with noise, the advantage no longer belongs to whoever speaks the loudest…

It belongs to whoever feels impossible to ignore.

Maybe that’s the real shift happening right now.

We’re moving from the era of aggressive acquisition…

into the era of perceived inevitability.

The companies that thrive next won’t just generate leads.

They’ll shape perception so effectively that trust already exists before the first touchpoint even happens.

That’s a very different game.

Je n’ai pas l’habitude de prendre la parole sur ce type de sujet ici sur LinkedIn. Pourtant, je suis convaincu qu’il est essentiel de s’exprimer sur cette question aujourd’hui.

Le Conseil d’État examine actuellement un projet de loi visant à revoir l’organisation des antennes locales de l'ADEME, en les rattachant aux DREAL (Directions régionales de l’environnement, de l’aménagement et du logement) et, de fait, en les plaçant sous l’autorité des préfets.

Cette réforme entraînerait un affaiblissement majeur de l’agence, notamment parce que :
1.  Le réseau régional sur lequel l’ADEME s’appuie pour faire avancer des milliers de projets locaux en faveur de l’écologie se retrouverait soumis au pouvoir hiérarchique des préfets. Les priorités ne seraient alors plus guidées par l’urgence écologique, mais davantage par celles du ministère de l’Intérieur.
2.  La suppression des agences territoriales provoquerait une dilution des compétences, de l’expertise et de l’efficacité des équipes, au sein de structures ne disposant ni du savoir-faire technique et scientifique nécessaire, ni de l’ancrage local auprès des élus et porteurs de projets.

Même si ces deux points peuvent paraître abstraits pour beaucoup, cette proposition est surtout le signe visible d’une intention plus large : affaiblir le rôle de l’ADEME, dénigrer son activité et minimiser sa contribution à l’avancement de la transition écologique.
L’ADEME, ce n’est pas seulement une institution. C’est un soutien concret à travers des financements pour des projets locaux, des ressources digitales, des études, des guides, des formations et des données accessibles librement.
Il est donc important que chacun — et encore plus les personnes dont le métier consiste à contribuer à la transition écologique — soit informé de ce qu’il se passe et prenne position.

Je fais donc appel à mon réseau, même modeste, pour mobiliser un maximum de personnes et alerter sur ce sujet.

Voici quelques actions concrètes possibles :
1. Écrire à vos sénateurs et députés locaux.
2. Relayer le sujet sur les réseaux sociaux et soutenir les publications existantes.
3. Diffuser l’appel à témoignages : https://lnkd.in/dgU5FCJf
4. Partager la tribune sur le sujet, déjà soutenue par plus de 400 signataires : https://lnkd.in/dQnB7-yc 
5. Utiliser le kit de mobilisation conçu par Gabrielle Piot pour faciliter le passage à l’action.


PS : Merci à toi Gabrielle d'avoir lancé cette mobilisation !!

2. Multicore Timing Analysis: Managing Interference Between Cores

Multicore processors are now standard in modern embedded systems, but with that comes the challenge of managing timing interference between cores. Shared resources like caches, memory controllers, and interconnects can create subtle timing interactions that are tough to spot using traditional approaches. Our latest announcement brings advanced worst-case timing coupling analysis and mitigation capabilities, helping engineering teams build more predictable and reliable systems.

Read More → Here

3. AI Supporting Verification and Validation

We've announced enhancements to the TASKING toolchain that bring AI into the full software development workflow, from design and compile right through to debug, test, and verification and validation. Using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), AI agents can securely interact with the toolchain and access the data they need to automate key tasks across the lifecycle. The idea is simple: let AI take care of the time-consuming, repetitive work so that engineers can focus on the things that really matter. Development teams can now build, verify, and validate complex systems faster, with less risk and at a lower cost.

#### これやんの作品コメント

日本画材を用いて古代生物の質感を表現する木下武先生。この作品では古代の海生爬虫類モササウルスが、海中を穏やかに泳ぐ姿を描いています。水面の揺らぎや鱗の凹凸が緻密に表現され、鱗には日本画材の雲母を用いていて、木下先生曰く“雲母の原料でもあるケイ酸塩は自然界の魚の鱗にも含まれているので、リアリティを出すためにシンクロさせてみました”とのこと。色彩が統一されているので絵肌の質感に自然と目が行く作品です。

### STORY

これやん：絵を描くようになったきっかけは？

木下：幼い頃に手にひどい火傷を負い、1ヵ月くらい療養をしました。そのときに時間を持て余して、絵を描き始めたのがきっかけでした。療養中にビデオで観た映画のワンシーンを思い出して描いたりしていました。

その後は小学生の頃からデッサンを習い、中学2年生の頃に絵描きになりたいと思っていました。美術科がある高校で出会った恩師に“木下は日本画のほうが合うと思う”と言われましたが、当時は油絵で人物画や自画像を描いていて、日本画や画材のことはよく知りませんでした。でも、恩師のことは信頼していたので、大学は藝大の日本画を目指しました。日本画材に触れたのは大学に入ってからでしたね。

これやん：実際に日本画の画材に触れてみて、どうでしたか？

木下：日本画材の原料でもある石や金属といった物質に、生で触れる感覚が自分には合っていました。もともと化石が好きだったこともあり、しっくりくるものがありました。在学中は画材や原料の研究をしていて、大学院に進むつもりが院生試験で不合格になり、どうしたら良いのか分からなくなって先生に理由を伺いにいきました。そうしたら“君は技術も知識も申し分ないが、本当はもっといろんなものを描けるんじゃないか？”と言われて。その言葉を機に、自分の視野が狭まっていたことに気が付き、大学4年生の終わり頃から描いていた生き物をモチーフにして、どうにか自分なりの作品を表現しようと思いました。

これやん：どのようにして今の画風に辿り着いたのですか？

木下：これまでにあまり取り組まれていない技法で表現をしたいと思っていました。素材は日本画材ですが、絵肌をやすりで削って仕上げたらどうなるのかと思ってはじめたのが今の手法です。最初に取り組んだモチーフはアンモナイトでした。岩絵の具自体が石の粉ですから、化石の物質感を強調した絵肌が作れるんじゃないかなと。まず絵具をモデリングのように重ねていき、殻や鱗など生き物の細かい質感を作ります。岩絵具は厚みがあるとヒビが入りやすくなるので、何層にも分けて塗ります。最後に目の細かい耐水性の紙やすりで磨き上げ、絵肌に艶を出します。この技法自体は油絵の下地作り（エマルジョン）の方法で、それを日本画材に応用しています。

これやん：話を聞いていて、木下さんの技法は工芸に近い感覚があるのかと思いました。作品を通して伝えたいことは何ですか？

木下：そうですね。私自身、日本画は絵画的な要素を多く含んだ工芸なのではないかと思っています。岩絵具のように地球上に何億年も存在する時間的な含みを持つ素材と、古代のモチーフを組み合わせることで面白いものが生まれるんじゃないかと思ってこの表現を続けています。伝えたいのは質感ですね。こういったモチーフが持つ雰囲気を表現するには質感が大切だと思っています。自分がイメージする質感を日本絵具でどこまで再現できるのか、今も挑戦を続けています。

Nishikata Film Review: Mabo as Tokichiro Kinoshita (マー坊の木下藤吉郎, 1938)

The early animated talkie Mabo as Tokichiro Kinoshita (マー坊の木下藤吉郎, Mābō no Kinoshita Tōkichirō, 1938) brings together a popular cartoon figure of the 1930s, the young boy hero Mābō (マー坊), and a legendary figure of Japanese history, Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1537-1598), who in his youth was known by the name Tōkichirō Kinoshita.

Hideyoshi was a great daimyō of the turbulent Sengoku Period. He was the second of three men known as the great “Unifiers of Japan” because of his role in bringing peace and stability to the region which was at the time in a state of constant civil war. Hideyoshi was an ideal hero for Japanese propaganda of the Fifteen Years’ War (1931-45), not only for his role as a unifier but also because of his hard stance against foreign religion. He notoriously ordered the execution by crucifixion of 26 Christians in Nagasaki in 1597, known as The 26 Martyrs of Japan.

As this is propaganda aimed at children, the unknown filmmakers have chosen to focus on the adventures of Hideyoshi’s youth when he was known as Tōkichirō Kinoshita. He is played by Mābō – a popular figure of the time in comics and animated shorts. It is not clear how many Mābō films were made – at least one other film that survives, Mābō’s Big Race(1936) shows Mābō competing for Japan at the Berlin Olympics. The makers of both films are currently uncertain, but it is clear that Mabo as Tokichiro Kinoshita is a more sophisticated short (either a different animator, or the animator has improved his skills in the intervening years) than the earlier film. Mābō looks very different in 16th century garb, but his face is recognisable with his snub nose, big ears, large eyes, slightly jutting chin and small, high eyebrows.

Having popular cartoon characters take on other roles is something that began early in animation. For example, Oswald the Lucky Rabbit, the precursor to Mickey Mouse, often takes on other roles. He’s a fire fighter in Fiery Fireman (1928) and in Yanky Clippers (1929) he’s a barber. One of my favourite examples of a popular cartoon character taking on another role is the much later film Mickey and the Beanstalk (1947) with Mickey replaying Jack in the famous English fairy tale. It’s a clever way to bring together the popularity of a character with a proven storyline. In the case of Hideyoshi, his exploits as a child had taken on a legendary status through retellings over the centuries.

Nishikata Film Review: Renzo & Sayoko Kinoshita

This month marks the 12th anniversary of the passing of independent animation pioneer Renzō Kinoshita (木下蓮三, 3 Sept. 1936 - 15th January 1997). Kinoshita, along with his wife and collaborator Sayoko (木下小夜子, b. 1945) made a number of internationally acclaimed films together and were the founders of the biannual Hiroshima International Animation Festival.

Kinoshita grew up in Osaka where, according to an interview with Sadao “Miyasan” Miyamoto (宮本貞雄), he did his training at a small animation studio. Later Miyamoto and Kinoshita would both work together on the Astro Boy series at Tezuka’s Mushi Productions in Tokyo. However, unlike Miyamoto, who would continue in mainstream animation (working on Gatchaman and later at Disney), Kinoshita grew weary of the constraints of commercial animation. He founded his own animation studio Studio Lotus (スタジオロータス) in 1967. I imagine that the name of the studio derives its inspiration from the kanji “ren” in his given name, which means “lotus”. In 1969 Sayako, whom Kinoshita had met at Mushi Pro, joined the production team at Studio Lotus, and they married soon after.

Kinoshita became well known in Japan in the late 1960s when he developed the character Geba Geba Ojisan (ゲバゲバおじさん) for the popular television series Kyosen x Maetake Geba-Geba 90-pun! (巨泉×前武ゲバゲバ90分!) on Nippon Terebi. This included a series of comical shorts as well as creating comedic sequences in which Geba Geba Ojisan interacts with the actors themselves. The history of using live action people in combination with animated characters dates back to the earliest animated films with Winsor McCay’s early short film Gertie the Dinosaur (1914) showing McKay interacting with Gertie. The comedic possibilities of live animation together with animation were proven by the popularity of Disney’s Alice Comedies in the 1920s. In this sequence from a Geba Geba Best Selection episode, Kinoshita has animated a dance sequence with the Geba Geba character and an actor in a style reminiscent of Gene Kelly dancing with Jerry Mouse in Anchors Aweigh (1945).

Along with his work for Nippon Terebi (ie. Karikyura Machine) in the 1970s, the Kinoshitas produced commercials in order to fund their most important work: the independent films. The first film that the couple made, with Sayako taken charge of the planning, scripting, animation, and production with Renzo did the key animation and direction, was Made in Japan. The film is a tongue-in-cheek criticism of post-war Japan and it won the Grand Prize at the New York International Film Festival. The Kinoshitas were buoyed by their success with the film abroad, and thought they could continue making such independent films back in Japan, but found little support for independent filmmakers at the time. This inspired them to focus not only on their own creative initiatives but also on fostering an independent filmmaking community in Japan.

Director Baku Kinoshita Discusses His Poetic Animated Feature 'The Last Blossom' - Japan Nihon

The Last Blossom is an animated feature that begins by connecting us to reality through the sound of a man’s breath. “Even before that breathing, we start with the image of a little insect,” notes Baku Kinoshita, the film’s writer-director. “And so you’ve got this creature of the natural world, and then human breathing. It’s a way of introducing the two motifs that we find throughout the film — nature and humanity.”

The Last Blossom marks Kinoshita’s debut feature film, which was introduced at Annecy last year and is currently making its way through international festivals. The film follows the tremendous success of Kinoshita’s anime mystery series Oddtaxi. While that series highlighted a diverse cast of anthropomorphic animals, The Last Blossom focuses on the life of one man living out his final days on death row.

Baku Kinoshita “This one was always going to have human characters,” Kinoshita explains. “But because Oddtaxi featured animals, I wanted to instead focus on plants in this one.” A critical moment from ex-yakuza Akutsu’s past is revealed through flashback. He appears blocky in design and wears a plain white t-shirt, resembling a mix between a character from a Takeshi Kitano film and Hank Hill from King of the Hill. “What’s important for me when designing characters in animation is to ‘abbreviate’ the designs,” Kinoshita explains. “To eliminate as many unnecessary elements as possible. In place of those additions, we use the animation of the face, the acting that comes through that, to express emotion.”

Opposite Akutsu are two key characters — Nana, the compassionate woman who takes him in, and Housenka, a plant that occasionally converses with him. Voiced by musician and character actor Pierre Taki, this comical plant adds a layer to the film. “When I watch [Taki], I can’t quite grasp his thoughts — he possesses a very human depth. So I offered him this role,” states Kinoshita. “Housenka has been alive for over a hundred years — he’s wiser than us. That enigmatic quality, which gives him a slightly god-like presence, resonates with the mystery I perceive in Pierre’s acting.”

The story concerns Inoue’s own childhood in Izu in the early Taisho period (1912-26) when Inoue was around seven years old, and the title refers to the white aphids that the children would try to catch in the autumn.

He’s all she’s got, so she spoils him, and he’s very attached to her as a result. The only other person he really likes is Sakiko (Izumi Ashikawa), whom he calls his elder sister although she’s actually his aunt. Sakiko lives in the ‘Upper House’ nearby with Kosaku’s other relations, but he feels uncomfortable there and avoids them. Martin Dowsing: Ryo Kinoshita

| Kyoko Kishida |
| --- |

Taeko (Kyoko ‘Woman of the Dunes’ Kishida) is a wealthy, aristocratic and self-confident Tokyo fashion designer who visits a gay bar, where she is attracted to younger, proletarian bartender Senkichi (Tsutomu Yamazaki, the kidnapper from High and Low), whom she asks out on a date. The rumour that he’ll sleep with absolutely anyone for money fails to put her off, but she’s taken aback when he turns up wearing geta (wooden sandals), chews with his mouth open and takes her to a pachinko parlour, but she soon gets over it and the two embark on a relationship. However, when her friends ask her if Senkichi is kind to her, she realises that she can’t think of a single example of his showing such a quality and begins to feel somewhat insecure in their relationship. But it turns out that Senkichi is actually far more conventional than he pretends to be…

| Tsutomu Yamazaki |
| --- |

This Toho production was based on a novel of the same name by Yukio Mishima first published in 1963 in serial form in a magazine called Mademoiselle. Although it has yet to be translated into English,* this appears to be a very faithful adaptation and Mishima is on record as being highly pleased with it. The author’s obsession with physical beauty and the psychology of infatuation are much in evidence, but the protagonists are both hard to like and I can’t say that I personally found the story very engaging. Most of the drama comes from the shifting balance of power in their relationship.

What really makes this film worth seeing, however, is the striking visual style that director Ryo Kinoshita (b.1931) and his cameraman Yuzuru Aizawa (who also shot The Bad Sleep Well) bring to it. Kinoshita was a former assistant to Yuzu Kawashima (and no relation to Keisuke Kinoshita as far as I’m aware). The rest of his brief filmography looks pretty routine, but he was one of those directors whose career began a little too late, leaving him few opportunities to show what he could do for the cinema before he was forced to move into television instead. In fact, part of the reason for the move in his case may have been that the bigwigs at Toho were, apparently, displeased with the arty visuals in The School of Flesh. However, in my opinion, the use of deep focus, unusual camera angles and bold lighting effects makes this film a visual treat throughout.

The age discrepancy between the two characters is less pronounced than in the book, which describes Taeko as being 39 and Senkichi 21 – at the time of the film’s release, Kishida was 34 and Yamazaki 28. The two stars had both been members of the Bungakuza theatre company and knew each other well. Another person associated with Bungakuza was Yukio Mishima himself – the company had staged a number of his plays, often featuring Kishida, an actress who was both admired and befriended by the writer.

*The novel has appeared in French and also provided the basis for the French film L’ecole

Saitō intègre les studios Nikkatsu, où il fait ses débuts au cinéma en 1925, avant de rejoindre Shochiku deux ans plus tard. How I Structured My Weeks at Amazon Amazon can feel like a constant stream of urgency. Escalations. Ad-hoc asks. Back-to-back meetings. Threads that multiply overnight. Early on, I realized something important: If I didn’t structure my week intentionally, the week would structure me. Over time, I built a rhythm that helped me stay ahead of the chaos. Here’s how I structured most weeks. 1/ Monday: Clarify what actually matters ↳ I started every week by identifying the 3 outcomes that had to move ↳ Not tasks. Outcomes. Examples: ↳ unblock legal approval ↳ align teams on launch scope ↳ finalize decision for leadership review If those three things moved, the week was productive. 2/ Tuesday–Wednesday: Deep work and program momentum ↳ These were my execution days ↳ Writing docs, resolving dependencies, driving alignment I tried to protect blocks of time for thinking and building, not just reacting. That’s where real progress happened. 3/ Thursday: Decision and escalation day ↳ By Thursday I knew where things stood So I focused on: ↳ resolving blockers ↳ escalating risks early ↳ framing tradeoffs for leadership The goal was to avoid surprises the following week. 4/ Friday: Reset the system ↳ I reviewed what actually moved ↳ captured open risks ↳ and defined the next week’s priorities That small reset made Monday far less chaotic. 5/ Every day: Protect signal from noise ↳ Urgent messages never stopped ↳ But I tried to constantly ask: “What actually moves the program forward?” Because at Amazon, progress wasn’t about activity. It was about momentum in the right places. Structure didn’t remove chaos. But it made chaos manageable. 📬 I write weekly about program management, leadership, and operating in high-pressure environments in The Weekly Sync: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e6qAwEFc How do you structure your week when things get hectic?

Donna Morris, Chief People Officer at Walmart

Walmart's Chief People Officer has said that the company is striving to develop a level of AI literacy in every area of its workforce

Donna Morris, Chief People Officer of Walmart, has said that the company is looking to develop some level of AI skills for every single one of its in-store and corporate employees.

Speaking at the MIT Technology Review’s EM Tech AI summit, Donna said that the company had been experimenting with AI use cases in recent years to streamline work and improve the customer experience – but stressed that having a thorough upskilling strategy was crucial.

“We need to bring people along on the journey, and we need to make sure that we’re educating people,” She told attendees. “It’s a form of literacy in many ways, and so we really want to make sure that our associates feel literate and capable of using AI.”

## AI reshaping at Walmart

According to Donna, the “vast majority,” or the company’s jobs will have some form of shaping as it brings in new AI capabilities.

To ensure employees are prepared, she advises that the team at Walmart remains “pragmatic about how much AI is truly shaping and what jobs.”

Managing this ‘shaping’ has involved the launch of an AI professional certificate through a partnership between Google and Walmart.

This certificate is designed to focus on the most critical areas of AI skills development for specific job roles – spanning communication, research, data analysis, planning and organisation and content generation.

Walmart employees also have access to practical, job-focused training as part of this partnership, which allows staff to experiment with AI skills in the context of their roles.

This is being rolled out to all staff, following Walmart’s integration of AI tools across the business – including on its shop floor, where it has introduced AI led task management to reduce shift planning time.

Donna said of the partnership: “We want to make sure that we equip all of our associates with the best tools to allow them to be successful as Walmart continues to reshape as a people-led, tech-powered company. But equally so that each of our associates has the ability to navigate their own careers.”

24th April 2026

Walmart is moving ahead with one of the most ambitious artificial intelligence workforce strategies in global retail, with plans to equip its entire 2.1 million-strong workforce with AI skills over the coming years as part of a wider transformation of how the business operates.

Speaking to Riad Beladi, Editor of International Supermarket News, at the IMT EmTech AI Summit, Donna Morris, Executive Vice-President and Chief People Officer at Walmart, outlined how the retailer is embedding AI across every layer of the organisation, from head office functions to frontline store associates.

Morris described Walmart as a “people-led, tech powered” business, highlighting how the company has been developing its AI strategy since the rise of generative AI in 2022. What initially began as internal experimentation has since evolved into a structured framework, with dedicated platforms enabling employees to explore and apply AI tools in practical working environments.

Today, Walmart operates multiple agent-based AI systems, combining proprietary developments with external large language models. These systems are designed to support a wide range of functions, from improving productivity and streamlining workflows to enhancing operational decision-making across stores and supply chains.

Morris told Riad Beladi that the central objective is to remove friction from employees’ daily tasks while ensuring that AI becomes an accessible and practical tool for all associates, not just those in technical roles. “We want AI to be something every associate can use with confidence to improve how they work and serve customers,” she said.

While Walmart employs more than 35,000 people within its technology division, Morris stressed that the ambition goes far beyond IT teams. The long-term strategy is to embed AI capability across the entire organisation, ensuring that digital skills become a core part of the workforce.

The initiative reflects a wider shift across global retail, where artificial intelligence is increasingly seen as a foundational skill rather than an optional tool. For Walmart, the focus is on preparing employees for a future in which human roles and AI systems operate more closely together to meet evolving customer expectations.

As competition intensifies across the retail sector, Walmart’s approach signals a decisive move towards a fully AI-enabled workforce, positioning the company at the forefront of technological transformation in global grocery retail.

Re-skilling Vs Hiring In This Disruptive Digital Era. AI, automation, and cloud technologies aren’t just transforming operations — they’re rewriting the rules of competition. According to McKinsey & Company, 30% of work could be automated by 2030, signalling a profound shift in workforce requirements and skills priorities. These digital shifts will render some roles redundant while widening critical skills gaps across the workforce. Failure to address these gaps organizations risk falling behind in an increasingly skills-driven economy. Today, the discussion between reskilling and hiring extends beyond workforce planning — it determines how quickly organizations execute strategy and sustain competitive advantage. Companies that rely solely on internal skills development risk lagging behind in markets where specialized expertise drives innovation. The Value of Employee Adaptability Technical skills become obsolete. Employee adaptability endures. In an AI-driven era, adaptability, curiosity, and problem-solving capacity are assets. Organizations that hire for technical fit and a progressive mindset while also investing in skills development build teams capable of evolving alongside technology. Hiring Right Is Now A Strategic Priority Today, I am increasingly interacting with clients who prefer engaging recruitment consultants when hiring employees. This is largely driven by the need to access pre-vetted talent quickly, especially when time sensitivity is critical during transformation initiatives or strategic projects. Organizations also face growing skill complexity, where internal teams may not be able to acquire specialized capabilities fast enough without affecting business outcomes. Recruitment consultants help bridge this gap by identifying technically qualified candidates who already possess the required expertise and a progressive mindset. At the same time, leaders must consider business risk. When capability gaps persist or internal teams cannot adapt quickly enough, strategic hiring becomes essential to maintain competitiveness, productivity, and innovation. Recruitment consultants help mitigate these risks by leveraging industry expertise and conducting informed candidate evaluations to identify the right talent. 📩 Reach out to me for a consultative discussion on how I can support your recruitment needs.#Recruitment#TalentStrategy#AIWorkforce#ReskillingHiring

Nathalie Scardino President & Chief People Officer April 29, 2026 3 min read

The old playbook for work is obsolete. I spend my days putting a new one into practice – actively dismantling legacy processes to redesign work for an agentic era. We are reskilling at scale and evolving our entire organization to turn technological advancement into a competitive advantage. We aren’t just transforming Salesforce; we are leading our customers through this same radical evolution.

The leaders who get this right understand one thing clearly: AI isn’t just a technology challenge – it’s a workforce strategy challenge. It’s the difference between AI transformation that works and AI investment that falls flat.

## The Front Door to the Agentic Enterprise: Slackbot

We believe the key to preparing people for this transformation is building AI fluency. This is why we have made Slack our system of engagement to bring AI capabilities to where work already happens.

Slackbot is the engine. It doesn’t just assist; it automates the heavy lifting of drafting, summarizing, researching, planning – completely redefining our daily output. It becomes not a new tool you need to master but rather an extension of how you do your job, as ubiquitous as email or mobile. It has the power to free up your time, creativity, and capacity to do truly meaningful work. With 100% of our employees now using AI agents – and every employee equipped with a personal AI agent through Slackbot – entirely new forms of work have emerged.

Software engineers are shifting from writing every line of code to directing AI systems that build it. Sales representatives who once spent hours filtering and researching leads now rely on AI agents for that groundwork, freeing them to focus entirely on high-value customer conversations.

When leaders rethink how tasks, roles, and AI systems interact, employees are able to focus more of their time on the uniquely human parts of work.

## Redesign Work for AI — Don’t Just Add It

Capturing the AI opportunity means moving beyond static role definitions and redesigning work at a more granular level. That’s why we created the 4Rs playbook to building an agentic workforce: Redesign how work gets done, reskill people with the top 10 skills for the agentic era, redeploy talent into growth areas, and rebalance to ensure humans and AI each focus on what they do best.

This framework has helped reimagine our organization. For example, by deploying Agentforce on our help site, we resolved the majority of customer questions autonomously, allowing us to redeploy hundreds of support engineers into net-new roles like AI conversation designers and forward-deployed engineers – fast growing parts of the business.

Dame Marjorie has been Chief Executive of Pearson, the international education and media business made up of Pearson Education, Penguin and the Financial Times Group, since 1997. Between 1985 and 1997 she was successively President of the Economist Newspaper Group Inc. and Chief Executive of the Economist Group. Prior to 1985, she was a partner in a law firm in Savannah, Georgia, and founded and published the Pulitzer Prize winning newspaper, The Georgia Gazette. She is a non-executive director of Nokia Corporation and a member of a number of charitable and advisory boards, including The MacArthur Foundation and The Carter Center.Scardino is married to journalist Albert Scardino; the Scardinos have three children.

It hasn't felt like a great year for women at the very top of British business. There have been some outstanding commercial results - Louise Makin at BTG and Kate Swann at WH Smith stand out - but the number of women CEOs has fallen. Marjorie Scardino left Pearson in late 2012 and Cynthia Carroll Anglo-America in February. Kate Swann has announced she will leave WH Smith in June this year after almost 10 years in which she has transformed the company's fortunes. These departures reduce the number of FTSE 350 companies led by women to 11, just 3% of the total ...

1. Louise Makin BTG
2. Angela Ahrendts Burberry
3. Dido Harding Talk Talk
4. Carolyn McCall Easy Jet
5. Ruby McGregor-Smith MITIE
6. Harriet Green Thomas Cook
7. Dorothy Thompson DRAX
8. Caroline Banszky Law Debenture
9. Alison Cooper Imperial Tobacco
10. Lyn Fordham SVG Capital
11. Katherine Garrett-Cox Alliance Trust

There are certainly some very able women serving as executive directors and particularly CFOs of FTSE 350 companies but there numbers are increasing very slowly. The % of women executive directors has increased from just 5.5% to 5.8% since the publication of the Davies Report in 2011. Only 8% of executive appointments over this period have been women. Unless we see significant growth in the number of women executive directors, it is very hard to see from where the next generation of women CEOs will come. เดม มาร์จอรี สคาร์ดิโน (นามสกุลเดิมมอร์ริส เกิดเมื่อวันที่ 25 มกราคม พ.ศ. 2490) เป็นผู้บริหารธุรกิจชาวอังกฤษเชื้อสายอเมริกัน เธอเป็นอดีตซีอีโอของเพียร์สัน พีแอลซี สคาร์ดิโนได้เป็นกรรมการของอ็อกซ์แฟมระหว่างดำรงตำแหน่งที่เพียร์สัน[2]

เธอถูกวิพากษ์วิจารณ์จาก นิตยสาร Private Eyeเนื่องจากในขณะที่ Oxfam รณรงค์ต่อต้านการหลีกเลี่ยงภาษีนิติบุคคล ในฐานะส่วนหนึ่งของ IF Coalition นั้น Pearson เป็น "ผู้ใช้แหล่งหลบเลี่ยงภาษีอย่างล้นหลาม ... โดยโอนเงินหลายร้อยล้านปอนด์ผ่านบริษัทในลักเซมเบิร์กที่ซับซ้อนหลายแห่ง (และสาขาในลักเซมเบิร์กของบริษัทในสหราชอาณาจักร) เพื่อหลีกเลี่ยงภาษี" [3] [4] [5]เธอกลายเป็นประธานเจ้าหน้าที่บริหารหญิงคนแรกของ บริษัท FTSE 100เมื่อเธอได้รับแต่งตั้งให้เป็นประธานเจ้าหน้าที่บริหารของ Pearson [6]ในปี 1997 เธอยังเป็นกรรมการที่ไม่เป็นผู้บริหารของ Nokiaและอดีตประธานเจ้าหน้าที่บริหารของ Economist Group [ 7] [8]ในช่วงเวลาที่เธออยู่ที่ Pearson กำไรของ Pearson เพิ่มขึ้นสามเท่าเป็นสถิติ 942 ล้านปอนด์[9]

ในเดือนธันวาคม พ.ศ. 2556 เธอเข้าร่วมคณะกรรมการของ Twitter, Inc.ในฐานะกรรมการหญิงคนแรก หลังจากเกิดข้อโต้แย้งเกี่ยวกับการขาดความหลากหลายในคณะกรรมการของ Twitter [10] [11]

## ชีวิตช่วงแรกและการศึกษา

สคาร์ดิโนเกิดที่เมืองแฟลกสตาฟ รัฐแอริโซนาในปี พ.ศ. 2490 และเติบโตที่เมืองเท็กซาร์คานา รัฐเท็กซัสขณะที่อาศัยอยู่ในรัฐเท็กซัส เธอได้เข้าร่วมการ แข่งขันขี่ม้าโรดิโอตั้งแต่ยังเป็นวัยรุ่น[12]สคาร์ดิโนสำเร็จการศึกษาจากมหาวิทยาลัยเบย์เลอร์สำเร็จการศึกษาระดับ ปริญญาตรีสาขาภาษาฝรั่งเศสและจิตวิทยาในปี พ.ศ. 2512 เธอเริ่มเรียนนิติศาสตร์ที่มหาวิทยาลัยจอร์จวอชิงตันแต่ลาออกกลางคันเพื่อไปเป็นนักข่าวที่สำนักข่าวเอพีในเมืองชาร์ลสตัน รัฐเวสต์เวอร์จิเนีย และต่อมาได้รับ ปริญญานิติศาสตรดุษฎีบัณฑิต (JD)จากคณะนิติศาสตร์ มหาวิทยาลัยซานฟรานซิสโก [ 13]

## อาชีพ

ก่อนปี 1985 Scardino เป็นผู้จัดพิมพ์ The Georgia Gazette

เธอเป็นประธานกรรมการ[14]ของมูลนิธิ MacArthurและสมาชิกคณะกรรมการของCarter Center [15]เธอเป็นสมาชิกกิตติมศักดิ์ของ Royal Society of Arts [ 13]เธอยังได้รับรางวัล Benjamin Franklin Medalใน ปี 2002 อีกด้วย [16]

ในปี พ.ศ. 2550 เธอถูกจัดให้อยู่ในอันดับที่ 17 ใน รายชื่อ 100 สตรีผู้ทรงอิทธิพลที่สุดในโลกของนิตยสาร Forbes [17]

เมื่อวันที่ 3 ตุลาคม 2012 มีการประกาศว่าเธอจะก้าวลงจากตำแหน่งซีอีโอของ Pearson และจะถูกแทนที่โดย John Fallon [ 18] [19]

ในเดือนธันวาคม พ.ศ. 2556 เธอได้เข้าร่วมคณะกรรมการของ Twitter, Inc. [10]ในฐานะกรรมการหญิงคนแรก หลังจากเกิดข้อโต้แย้งเกี่ยวกับการขาดความหลากหลายในคณะกรรมการของ Twitter [11]

## ชีวิตส่วนตัว

สคาร์ดิโนแต่งงานกับอัลเบิร์ต สคาร์ดิโน [ 8]ซึ่งเธอเคยร่วมงานด้วยในช่วงที่อยู่ที่เดอะจอร์เจียกาเซ็ตต์และต่อมาเป็นนักข่าวของเดอะนิวยอร์กไทมส์เธอมีลูกสามคน ได้แก่ แอดิเลด วิล และฮาล(โปรดิวเซอร์และอดีตนักแสดงเด็ก) [20]

# ESCP exits X (formerly Twitter)

The General Committee of ESCP has decided to leave X, the social media platform formerly known as Twitter.

Early 2024 many universities have decided to leave X, citing declining relevance and reduced engagement. We have noted that the number of content moderators has been seriously decreased, leading to an increase in fake news and more hatred inducing posts.

The changes to Platform X—from the algorithmic amplification of right-wing populist content to the restriction of organic reach—make its continued use unacceptable for ESCP. The Society’s withdrawal underscores our commitment to fact-based communication and our opposition to anti-democratic forces. The values that promote diversity, freedom, and science are no longer upheld on the platform.

We want to reaffirm the importance of an open and constructive culture of debate. This decision applies exclusively to our X account and does not affect our communication via other social media channels, of which we will continue to closely monitor the development of the platforms and their algorithms.

A well-deserved moment to reflect — and a marker of how far the conversation has genuinely moved. Having worked alongside Goldman Sachs and other leading institutions on Project Inception — one of the earliest serious attempts to map the real roadblocks to institutional DLT adoption as Financial Market Infrastructure — the shift you describe from 'if' to 'how' is not just a market sentiment change. It's the result of hard, unglamorous work done by institutions willing to engage with the governance, legal finality, and operational trust questions that the technology alone couldn't answer. What Project Inception made clear early was that the barrier was never really the blockchain. It was the absence of a credible governance layer — who holds the levers, who is accountable in a stress event, and how exception doctrine maps to regulated functions. The fact that those questions are now being answered in production, not just in whitepapers, is what's driving the commercial momentum the market is seeing. Excited to see where the next phase takes you and the market. The foundations were hard won.

# IBM CHRO: Focus on AI productivity at your own risk

Exclusively pursuing AI for productivity gains will lead to strategy design that overlooks the tech’s true potential to drive enterprise growth, says IBM CHRO Nickle LaMoreaux.

- Contact Us
- HRM Asia Newsroom
- April 21, 2026

The word “productivity” has likely surfaced in more workforce strategy meetings than ever before during recent months, as business leaders press for transformation to maximise efficiencies and enable talent in an AI-powered world.

Nickle LaMoreaux, IBM’s CHRO

Yet, AI strategy that is guided only by a pursuit of productivity will miss the mark, says Nickle LaMoreaux, IBM’s CHRO. In remarks at The Wall Street Journal’s recent inaugural CPO Council Summit in Palo Alto, California, LaMoreaux, the 2024 HR Executive of the Year, says many organisations are thinking of AI transformation at the individual process level: How can the tech help employees write emails, gather insights, generate ideas—ultimately, how can AI drive productivity in employees’ daily tasks?

However, she advocates for HR taking a broader view. “Where we as CPOs can get the biggest bang for the buck is figuring out how we can put AI, technology and automation into enterprise workflows,” she says. The ways employees access customer support, how managers run the promotions process, and how HRBPs answer questions, “these are the workflows we should be focused on,” LaMoreaux says.

Transforming such processes through AI will indeed increase productivity, but it can also move the organisation towards measurable enterprise growth, which LaMoreaux says needs to be the real aim of AI integration.

Reimagining for reinvestment

As AI and automation make their way into the workplace, the impact on productivity is undoubtedly transforming conversations on workforce planning, as evidenced by the ongoing waves of mass layoffs.

LaMoreaux, however, challenges HR to think differently about AI’s potential. What if, in three years, AI could power 50% of the work currently done by humans in your organisation, but you had to keep your headcount flat, or even double it? What new products could you build? Which new clients could you go after with that freed-up manpower?

AI certainly drives efficiencies, leading to productivity and cost savings—LaMoreaux points to the US$4.5 billion in free cash flow from IBM’s own AI journey over the last three years—but it is not just a shot straight to the bottom line. To capture the full savings and promote real growth, HR has to also focus on how human talent will be reinvested.

“What growth can AI drive? What can we do differently?” LaMoreaux asks. Those are ideas she says many organisations are not focused on, which puts them at risk of “missing the moment.”

I’m excited to share that our latest research paper, “Sickle Cell Vaso-Occlusive Episodes Correlate with the Magnetic Heterogeneity of Red Blood Cells,” has been published in Blood Advances. In this study, we explored whether the magnetic properties of red blood cells—driven by differences in hemoglobin oxygenation states—can serve as biophysical markers of disease severity in sickle cell disease. Using single-cell analysis through cell tracking velocimetry, we found that the most magnetically extreme RBC populations (top and bottom 1%) correlate strongly with pain severity, particularly during vaso-occlusive episodes. # Optimized Meeting Room Scheduling with Heaps

Payal Kumari

𝐃𝐚𝐲 𝟒𝟒/𝟗𝟎 | 𝐌𝐞𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐨𝐨𝐦𝐬 𝐈𝐈𝐈 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰𝐬| 𝐃𝐒𝐀 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐉𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐲 Today I studied the problem 𝐌𝐞𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐑𝐨𝐨𝐦𝐬 𝐈𝐈𝐈 and focused on understanding how the solution moves from a simple idea to a more efficient one. First I looked at the brute force approach. The idea is to check every room for each meeting and assign the room if it is free. This works for small inputs but becomes slow when the number of meetings grows. The key observation is that we repeatedly need the earliest available room. Once this idea becomes clear, heaps make the solution easier to manage. The optimized solution uses two heaps. One heap keeps track of available room numbers. Another heap keeps track of ongoing meetings based on their ending time. When a meeting ends, the room becomes free again. If all rooms are busy, the meeting waits until the earliest room becomes available. This approach improves the solution to O(n log n). Today’s learning reminded me that many scheduling and resource problems follow the same pattern. If we need to repeatedly find the earliest available resource, heaps are often the right tool. Slowly building the habit of thinking about the problem first before jumping to code. Opay Digital Services Ltd., one of Nigeria’s leading digital payments platforms, has engaged top Wall Street banks Citigroup, Deutsche Bank, and JPMorgan Chase to prepare for an initial public offering in the United States, according to a report by Bloomberg. The SoftBank backed company is targeting a valuation of approximately $4 billion for the listing, which could take place later in 2026. This would represent a significant premium to its previous $2 billion valuation from a 2021 Series C funding round led by SoftBank’s Vision Fund and a step up from an implied valuation of around $3.1 billion at the end of 2025. Opay operates as a fintech “super app” in Nigeria, offering mobile money transfers, bill payments, merchant services, debit cards, and other financial products. The Lagos-based platform has experienced rapid growth in Africa’s largest economy, benefiting from the expansion of digital payments amid limited banking infrastructure. Reports indicate Opay has surpassed 20 million daily active users in recent periods, with strong transaction volumes and progress toward sustained profitability. The company has raised roughly $570 million to date, with SoftBank as a prominent investor alongside others such as Meituan, Source Code Capital, and IDG Capital. Early backer Opera, the Norwegian browser company that helped incubate Opay, recently valued its stake in a way that implied an enterprise value of about $3.1 billion for the fintech. A US listing would mark a notable milestone for African fintech and provide Opay with access to deeper capital markets and global investor interest in high-growth payments businesses. It would also follow SoftBank’s recent successful (though ultimately priced below range) US IPO of its Japanese payments unit PayPay earlier in 2026. Details of the offering size, exact timeline, and final valuation remain subject to market conditions and regulatory approvals. No formal SEC filing has been disclosed yet, and the plans are still in early preparation stages. The hiring of three major global banks signals Opay’s serious intent to pursue a Nasdaq listing and reflects growing confidence in the maturation of profitable or near-profitable African tech companies. Opay did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Welcome to this week’s episode of: What I Vibecoded I built a small Go library that pulls basic data from the Medtronic CareLink cloud portal. For those who don’t know, I’m a Type 1 diabetic and use an insulin pump. CareLink stores some of the pump’s data in the cloud. I wanted a simple way to access that data programmatically so I can use it in small future projects. This repo is an early step toward that. https://lnkd.in/gg_mQhFX The original inspiration was CareLink Bridge, which was built in Node. # Ghana to honour Christina Hammock Koch for historic Artemis II mission
Emmanuel Tetteh•4d ago•377 words · 2 min read
Share[]()[]()[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://ghanafront.com/article/ghana-to-honour-christina-hammock-koch-for-historic-artemis-ii-mission)[]()Copy article link
Summary
**Christina Hammock Koch** will be honored at a mutually agreed time by **President John Dramani Mahama** on behalf of the Ghanaian people. The Government of Ghana conveyed this intention through diplomatic channels. **Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa**, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, congratulated the astronauts of the **Artemis II** mission, describing their journey as "scientifically groundbreaking and exceedingly inspiring."
**Mr. Ablakwa** praised the team for undertaking the farthest ever journey from Earth and returning safely. He highlighted their achievement as a demonstration of "the boundless potential of human ingenuity and courage." **Christina Hammock Koch**, who studied at the University of Ghana and proudly maintains her association with the country, will be recognized for her remarkable accomplishments in space exploration. **Mr. Ablakwa** emphasized that **Koch's** achievement represents a source of national pride for Ghana, showcasing the global impact of Ghanaians in science and technology.
The **Artemis II** mission launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard the Space Launch System (**SLS**) rocket, carrying four astronauts in the Orion spacecraft. The crew members include **Reid Wiseman** (Commander), **Victor Glover** (Pilot), **Christina Hammock Koch** (Mission Specialist), and **Jeremy Hansen** (Mission Specialist from the Canadian Space Agency). The astronauts undertook a lunar flyby, travelling farther from Earth than any humans have since the Apollo missions, testing the Orion spacecraft in deep space while conducting experiments and monitoring systems. After completing the flyby, the crew entered the return trajectory and safely re-entered Earth's atmosphere, landing successfully.
Quick Summary
Ghana's government is preparing to recognize an astronaut from the Artemis II mission- a journey hailed as scientifically groundbreaking. The planned honour hints at a deeper connection between the astronaut and the nation, raising questions about Ghana's role in space exploration.

The Billionaire Balance Sheet: Formula One Teams When people think about the balance sheet of the ultra-wealthy, they often picture yachts, private jets, or trophy real estate. But one of the most fascinating assets in billionaire circles is something far more unusual: A Formula One team. Owning an F1 team sits at the intersection of sport, technology, global branding, and finance. There are only 10 teams on the grid, making it one of the most exclusive asset classes in the world. Over the past decade, the economics of Formula One have transformed. New cost caps, global media growth, and the sport’s rising popularity, particularly in the United States, have dramatically increased franchise values. Today, an F1 team is more than a racing operation. It’s: • A global marketing platform • A hub of cutting-edge engineering and technology • A rare scarcity asset in the world of sports ownership Race weekends bring together heads of state, Fortune 500 CEOs, sovereign wealth funds, and family offices in a single paddock. In that sense, a Formula One team is not just an investment. It’s a seat at one of the most exclusive tables in global sport and business.

Today, World Kidney Day 2026 marks the 20th anniversary of this global campaign. It is a moment to reaffirm AstraZeneca’s shared commitment to preventing kidney disease, promoting early detection, and advancing care that is sustainable and people-centred. Around the world, chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects nearly 850 million people and is projected to become the 5th leading cause of death by 2040. The progression of this disease places a profound burden on patients, families, caregivers, and health systems. Locally, the challenge is significant with the prevalence of CKD in Malaysia was 15.5% in 2018, an increase from 9.1% in 2011 among adults aged 18 years and above. The prevalence of CKD Stage 3–5 is expected to rise by 25%, further increasing the healthcare burden. The economic impact is also considerable. On average, each dialysis patient spends RM29,000–33,600 per year on treatment, with the total cost of CKD and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) projected to exceed RM4 billion by 2024, according to the Ministry of Health. Yet awareness remains alarmingly low with fewer than 10% of people know they have CKD. This is a call to act, and to act now. At AstraZeneca, we are committed to addressing major health challenges like CKD through an ongoing initiative for early screening. In 2025, we partnered with key retail pharmacies, medical societies, and diagnostics providers to empower patients, reaching approximately 1 million people and screening and referring around 10,000 patients. We are also advancing guideline implementation and policy efforts, including Kidney Risk Failure Equation (KFRE) automation within the laboratory reporting system, to enhance early CKD identification and enable timely interventions that can help delay progression to ESRD. There is clear momentum at AstraZeneca to reach new heights in delivering Ambition 2030, transforming kidney health and reducing the proportion of patients who develop kidney failure by 33%. Our integrated portfolio supports care across the cardio-renal-metabolic continuum care and focuses on slowing the progression of chronic kidney disease, helping people with type 2 diabetes protect their kidneys, keeping potassium levels in a safe range, and lowering the chance of heart complications for those with kidney problems. On this World Kidney Day, let us come together to raise awareness, champion policies that enable earlier detection and treatment, and work collectively toward a healthier and more sustainable future for all.#WorldKidneyDay

If it happens, brands like Hellmann’s, Knorr, Marmite, and Colman’s could all move into new hands. What stands out to me is that this is far bigger than a typical acquisition. It feels like a real strategic reset on both sides. Unilever continues to sharpen its focus around beauty and personal care, while McCormick would be making a huge statement about where it wants to play globally and how quickly it wants to scale. This is also not a new approach for McCormick. Some of its best known brands have been acquired rather than built organically, and that tells you a lot about how the biggest players are choosing to grow. If this deal goes through, it would be a landmark move and could significantly reshape the global condiments and flavourings category. The broader question for me is still the same though. That mindset is most visible right now in how we’re approaching innovation. We’ve already seen some other big wins that prove our people are taking the chance to be responsible with AI seriously.

But underneath that sits a broader shift: expanding our GenAI capabilities (including GenAI as a service), richer workforce insights through GenBI, and a clear focus on responsible and sustainable AI with the right guardrails in place. Even building up a network takes time, and often it's not clear to the academic that the time invested now will pay any dividends. February was one of those months that reminds me why curiosity matters – constantly asking the practical question of ‘how can we be better?’ – and why it’s key to keep improving for our customers, our colleagues, and for the future we’re shaping.

### Staying curious about AI

That mindset is most visible right now in how we’re approaching innovation. Over recent months, our AI learning across Lloyds Banking Group has accelerated rapidly – from our regular AI Ninja mentorship for our leaders to the recent launch of the AI Academy for all colleagues – where in its first two weeks of the launch, over 13,000 of our colleagues had completed a module to help their individual journeys with AI. We’ve already seen some other big wins that prove our people are taking the chance to be responsible with AI seriously.

But underneath that sits a broader shift: expanding our GenAI capabilities (including GenAI as a service), richer workforce insights through GenBI, and a clear focus on responsible and sustainable AI with the right guardrails in place. I’m excited to see how innovation is becoming part of how we lead, simplify and deliver better outcomes for customers, not something bolted on.

In 2025, we supported £17bn of lending to first‑time buyers and delivered £3.2bn of new finance to social housing. Since 2022, we’ve provided £70.9bn in sustainable finance, while continuing to reduce our own environmental impact – cutting direct carbon emissions by 56%, operational waste by 82%, and water use by more than half. These outcomes are the result of long‑term choices, sustained investment, and the everyday work of teams right across the Group.

Our pay gap reporting shows continued progress too – with reductions in both gender and ethnicity pay gaps – but it also reinforces something we’re very open about: there is still more to do. Pay gaps disappear when representation improves at senior levels, when progression pathways are fair and transparent, and when accountability is built into how we hire, develop and reward talent.

A proposed class-action lawsuit against Equifax Canada is raising some interesting questions about how credit data is accessed and shared in Canada. According to a recent report by Daily Hive, the case alleges that a Canadian’s credit file was repeatedly accessed through third-party platforms without their knowledge or consent. Many Canadians probably assume their credit file is only accessed when they apply for a loan or credit card. But behind the scenes, there’s an entire ecosystem of fintech apps and financial platforms connected through APIs and authentication systems that can request data in milliseconds. The reality is that most consumers don’t understand how these integrations actually work - or how widely their financial data may be circulating across platforms like Borrowell, Credit Karma, ClearScore, etc. Credit reporting plays an important role in lending, but stories like this highlight a bigger issue: transparency. # Κοκκίνου για Μαρινέλλα: «Πάντα όταν την έβλεπα, γονάτιζα στα πόδια της, σαν να ήμουν ένα πολύ μικρό παιδάκι, πολύ μικρή μπροστά της»

30 Μάρ 2026 Mon, 30 Mar 2026 02:18:00 +0300 02:18 Patras Events

Όλος ο κόσμος έχει ταραχτεί, εμείς οι καλλιτέχνες ίσως λίγο περισσότερο

Δηλώσεις στην εκπομπή «Σαββατοκύριακο παρέα» και τη Μαρία Κοκολάκη παραχώρησε ηΈλλη Κοκκίνου, η οποία μίλησε για τη Μαρινέλλα, που έφυγε χθες από τη ζωή.

«Λίγα λόγια για τη Μαρινέλλα δεν αρκούν, φυσικά δεν μπορώ να πω πολλά. Όλος ο κόσμος έχει ταραχτεί, εμείς οι καλλιτέχνες ίσως λίγο περισσότερο. Εγώ προσωπικά μεγάλωσα με τη μορφή της, με τη μουσική της, με τη μαγική, ανεπανάληπτη, εκφραστική φωνή της. Τη θυμάμαι σαν τώρα, όταν ήμουν κοριτσάκι, να τη βλέπω στις ελληνικές ταινίες. Ήταν η πρώτη μου αγάπη αυτή. Μόνο να τη λατρέψεις μπορούσες.

Η φωνή της, η προσωπικότητά της, η μοναδικότητά της, η αγάπη της για τον κόσμο, η αγάπη της για αυτό που έκανε. Ήταν μια αιώνια έφηβη. «Έφυγε» όπως εκείνη ήθελε, με ένα μικρόφωνο στο χέρι, πάνω στη σκηνή που υπεραγαπούσε, μαζί με τον κόσμο που υπεραγαπούσε, που ήθελε πάρα πολύ να δίνει στον κόσμο», είπε αρχικά η Έλλη Κοκκίνου.

Η Έλλη Κοκκίνου είπε στη συνέχεια: «Ήταν η τελευταία φορά που εμφανίστηκε, που είχα πάει στο Nox, την είχα δει. Και αυτό που θυμάμαι ήταν ότι πήγα στα καμαρίνια… Πάντα όταν την έβλεπα, γονάτιζα στα πόδια της, σαν να ήμουν ένα πολύ μικρό παιδάκι, πολύ μικρή μπροστά της.

Πάντα μου χάιδευε το κεφάλι και τους ώμους, γέλαγε με αυτό που έκανα εγώ. Εγώ το έκανα γιατί ήθελα να τη νιώσω πολύ κοντά μου και λόγω σεβασμού. Και δάκρυζα, από πολύ μικρή την έβλεπα και δάκρυζα. Πόσο μάλλον όταν την έβλεπα προσωπικά».

## Why she is suitable for you

Maria Krokou is a Psychologist – Psychotherapist, currently running a private practice at Kotzia Square, in the center of Athens. She graduated with distinction (grade: 8/10) from the Department of Psychology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, having been awarded a merit-based scholarship following an entrance examination. During her studies, she completed part of her academic training through an Erasmus scholarship at the Autonomous University of Madrid, where she focused on cognitive and behavioral techniques. In parallel, she participated for one year in the psychoeducational program of the Madrid City Council, Educamoscontigo, offering weekly online psychological support sessions to a secondary school student. She later completed a practical training program, also through an Erasmus scholarship, at the Las Torrecillas Therapeutic Educational Center of the NGO DIANOVA España, where she conducted psychoeducational classroom interventions as well as individual and group psychotherapy with adolescents facing recent addiction-related and emotional difficulties.
